article_text:
Peter Medak , the award-winning Hungarian-British film and television director with a career spanning six decades and credits including The Changeling starring George C. Scott, Romeo Is Bleeding with Gary Oldman and The Krays starring Martin and Gary Kemp, died Tuesday, October 27 in Los Angeles. He was 88.

His death was announced by family. Though a cause was not stated, the family noted that Medak died peacefully.

Born in Budapest, Hungary in 1937, Medak showed interest in movie-making by the time he was eight years old when his aunt gave him a 35-millimeter hand-cranked projector and a piece of film. At 13, under the Communist regime, he was banned from going to school, later saying, “my father was a so-called capitalist…he was… put away to prison for years. … I spent an awful lot of time on my own, in our apartment, because my father was in prison, my mother was working in a plastics factory, I had a brother who died. …I became an observer… you know, looking through this incredible keyhole of our apartment.”

After fleeing to England in 1956 at 18, Medak started as a trainee at Associated British-Pathe, and worked on the sets of major British productions while soon getting promoted to assistant director on films such as The Great Armored Car Swindle (1961) and The Phantom of the Opera (1962). MCA Universal Pictures quickly noticed his work and in 1963, and he was brought to Los Angeles and signed to a television-directing contract, working on the series Court Martial.

In 1967 Paramount signed him to direct his first feature, Negatives , with Glenda Jackson. His next two films were the highly acclaimed black comedies A Day in the Death of Joe Egg (1972), starring Alan Bates, and The Ruling Class (1972), with Peter O’ Toole, for which Medak was nominated for the Palme D’Or, and O’Toole was nominated for an Academy Award.

Medak earned a reputation across his six-decade career as an “actors’ director,” resulting in 27 features with such acclaimed films as The Changeling (1980) with George C. Scott; The Krays (1990); Let Him Have It (1991), and Romeo is Bleeding (1993), with Gary Oldman. His 2018 documentary The Ghost of Peter Sellers received acclaim, winning Best Documentary at the Beverly Hills Film Festival.

His prolific television directing work included of Homicide: Life on the Street, Chicago Hope, The Wire and Breaking Bad . With a deep interest in music, he directed some of the earliest music videos for artists such as Peter Gabriel and Pink Floyd, and, in the opera realm, directed La voix humaine with Julia Migenes. He staged a production of Salome in Minneapolis and Rigoletto with the Los Angeles Opera.

In a career spanning 60 years, making both cult and critically acclaimed movies, Medak directed 27 features and 59 episodes of television.

“If it’s in your blood, directing,” he said once. “You never stop directing and it doesn’t matter that you’re alone in your mind, dreaming or imagining things but you’re always making a movie.”

Medak is survived by his children Christopher, Joshua, Karen and Cornelia Medak and grandchildren Sacha, Marlowe, Ryden, Oliver and Anders.

He was previously married to Katherine La Kermance, Carolyn Seymour and Julia Migenes, and was in a relationship with Christine Wagner.

article_text:
The New Museum has unveiled the artists and collectives participating in the sixth edition of its Triennial, set to take place from 4 February until 16 May 2027.

The New Museum Triennial was established in 2009 as a recurring international exhibition dedicated to early-career artists. Entitled The Outside Expands , the 2027 exhibition will bring together 36 artists and collectives from 34 countries, including Mandy El-Sayegh, Nour Jaouda and Fehras Publishing Practices, with the most expansive international representation so far. It will also be the first edition to take place in the museum’s newly opened, OMA-designed expansion.

Co-curated by Vivian Crockett and Isabella Rjeille, The Outside Expands takes part of its inspiration from a 1979 intervention by Brazilian collective 3NÓS3 and X Galería, which placed duct-taped Xs over the entrances of multiple São Paulo galleries. Accompanied by a message, “What is inside remains, what is outside expands,” which questioned the boundaries of cultural institutions during Brazil’s civil-military dictatorship. It also references artist and writer Jota Mombaça’s 2018 intervention in Rio de Janeiro, in which the phrase “What has no space is everywhere” was cut from a temporary museum wall, leaving its absence visible. The “X” also refers more generally to a crossroads and a space for reflection and decisions.

These references inform the triennial’s consideration of how artistic practices can challenge established boundaries around territory, gender and identity, while opening up possibilities for alternative forms of collaboration.

article_text:
M edieval knights used to joust on warhorses with wooden lances, but this week in east London , two men jousted on Lime bikes with PVC pipes. This contemporary spin on a medieval spectacle is just one example of the spirit of the middle ages erupting into the zeitgeist.

As part of Frieze art fair, the artist Corbin Shaw staged a show called Feast of Fools. The “‘anti-Frieze” Frieze show took inspiration from a medieval festival where, as Shaw put it to GQ , “the peasant class could insult the rich”. In the video for Troye Sivan’s latest song, Party, the Australian pop star postures as a medieval knight.

On catwalks at Givenchy, Louis Vuitton and Max Mara , from wimples to chainmail, it’s been called “medievalcore”. In the new film The Uprising, actor Andrew Garfield has been leading the rabble in Paul Greengrass’s retelling of the Peasants’ Revolt. Sports Banger, the political collective that makes punchy T-shirts, has offerings that read: “ Peasants’ Revolt 1381. Let’s finish the job ”.

Why is the medieval era being mined by contemporary culture? Simon Trafford, a senior lecturer in medieval history at the University of London Institute of Historical Research, says “it’s always there”, but it’s more “a matter of which particular bit of it we decide to borrow from at any one time”.

“Some of the way modern artists and fashion designers are using the medieval is focused on joy and playfulness,” says Marion Turner, a professor of English literature and language at the University of Oxford. They’re not, she adds, “saying: ‘This is what I actually think the medieval world was like.’”

Bridget Dalton, a semiotician and cultural analyst at Truth Consulting, says: “It’s fun. It can be camp and it can be macho and it can be sexy as well.” In the video for Party, a victorious, post-battle Sivan gallops to celebrate with a hedonistic, homoerotic knees-up in a castle. In one piece of choreography, Sivan is used like a battering ram.

Dalton describes another emerging medieval strand as “wenchcore”, which offers “a more acceptable voracious sexuality, the ribald, singing, dancing, drinking, doesn’t-need-to-be-perfect idea of womanhood and of masculinity … more of just whatever goes”. It could be seen as the perfect, medieval-inflected answer to Brat. The middle ages, says Trafford, “gives us a sort of fantasy other space”.

Many buzzy modern ideas feel medieval-tinged: seasonality, an emphasis on nature, folklore and locality, which take on different emphases in our technological, globalised times. Community, is a focal point in much of this contemporary medievalism. The joust in London was geared towards accessibility in the week that Frieze, described by 24-year-old jousting artist Jack Cardenas “expensive and inaccessible”, took place. “So many members of the community came out,” he says.

There’s also an anti-authoritarian streak in medievalism, from Shaw to The Uprising in which a Ploughman takes his grievances to London in a move to restore egalitarianism to 14th-century England. With its own “no kings” moment, Garfield told the Washington Post recently he saw it as “prescient and kind of predictive” of the No Kings movement in the US.

There is, says Turner, an “interesting parallel” in the pandemic. “After the plague swept across Europe, there was massive social change, prompted by population decline, wage rises and new social mobility.” The peasants’ revolt “is absolutely that generation after the plague”. In the UK, in the post-Covid era, “people feel like they just don’t want to put up with what they used to put up with before the pandemic”.

Another parallel could be the advent of printing then versus the advent of the internet and AI now. For Turner, “AI is more extreme in its negative effects, but again there are parallels with the squashing of individual creativity by big technology”.

While rightwing politics often looks back to the middle ages for its own ends, within today’s youth-centric medievalism there’s a reclamation of the symbols of Englishness. As Shaw, whose cult-favourite T-shirt reads “Eng ‘lish’”, told GQ: “I hate the ruling classes of England , but there’s a lot of reasons to be proud to be English, we have to take these symbols back.”

According to Dalton, “watching youth culture embrace the medieval is a way to talk about Britain without flying a St George. It’s a very interesting route to reparative ideas about what it means to be British.”

For Trafford, “you will always be able to cherrypick … the little bits that play to your cause.” Marine Le Pen might be drawing on Joan of Arc as “this massively militant Christian figure”, while “you can definitely find that more friendly, more conducive society if you happen to be a leftwing person.” There’s a medievalism for everyone.

ユアサエボシと戦後アヴァンギャルドの変身寓話集 2026年10月31日（土）–12月27日（日） 練馬区立美術館 https://www.neribun.or.jp/museum.html 開館時間：10:00–18:00（入館は17:30まで） 休館日：月（ただし、11/23は開館）、11/24 企画担当：木下紗耶子（練馬区立美術館学芸員） 展覧会URL： https://www.neribun.or.jp/event/detail_m.cgi?id=202608151786784919

練馬区立美術館では、現代美術家の ユアサエボシ と、戦後の日本でアヴァンギャルド芸術を志した 池田龍雄 、 高山良策 、 中村宏 らの作品を「変身」をキーワードに紹介する「ユアサエボシと戦後アヴァンギャルドの変身寓話集」を開催する。 ユアサエボシ（1983年千葉県生まれ）は、古い雑誌や新聞、インターネットをもちいて集めたイメージを組み合わせて絵画を制作するとともに、「大正生まれの架空の三流画家 ユアサヱボシ」（1924-1987）の生涯の物語を創作して発表してきた。過去のイメージに着想を得て描くことで架空の物故画家「ヱボシ」へと変身することから自身を「擬態派」と呼び、「ヱボシ」が生きたという戦後と現代を往還することを試みている。本展で発表される新作にあわせて「ヱボシ」の年譜には新たな出来事が書き加えられ、作品にまつわる新たな物語が明らかになる。近年の主な展覧会に、個展「ユアサエボシ｜でいかい」（ギャラリー小柳、東京、2025）、グループ展「開館30周年記念 MOTコレクション マルチプル_セルフ・ポートレイト」（東京都現代美術館、2025）、グループ展「積層する時間：この世界を描くこと」（金沢21世紀美術館、石川、2025）などがある。

第二次世界大戦後、アヴァンギャルドの作家たちは、傷ついてゆがめられた人間やキメラ的な怪物、不気味な仮面などのイメージをとおして、戦争の記憶や戦後社会の矛盾、人間像の変容を描き出した。これらの表現は、シュルレアリスムやルポルタージュ絵画運動に関心を寄せた作家たちの現実への深い洞察から生み出されている。見慣れた姿からの変身や変形を描くことによって、作家たちはその背景にある出来事を寓話的に伝える独自の表現世界を切りひらいた。 本展では、同館収蔵作家である池田、高山、中村と、彼らの表現に着目してきたユアサに加え、 芥川（間所）紗織 、 桂ゆき 、 鶴岡政男 、 古沢岩美 を紹介する。戦後美術における「変身」のモチーフの広がりをたどることは、イメージをつうじた過去との対話のあらたな機会となる。また、小説家の小川哲（1986年生まれ）が特別協力し、架空の詩人による「ユアサヱボシ」の絵画の秘密にかかわる詩を発表する。

出品作家 ユアサエボシ、池田龍雄、高山良策、中村宏、芥川（間所）紗織、桂ゆき、鶴岡政男、古沢岩美

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "比利时艺术家卡斯滕·霍勒（Carsten Höller）巨大的盘旋银色滑梯已亮相墨西哥城波兰科的开放艺术空间（Arte Abierto Polanco），成为一项永久装置作品。", "links": [{"text": "Carsten Höller", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/carsten-holler/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这件大型装置作品题为《墨西哥城滑梯》（Mexico City Slides，2026），包含四条螺旋滑梯，与安塔拉（Antara）融为一体——这是一个集零售、餐饮、娱乐、办公和公共空间于一体的高档露天购物中心。霍勒的这件装置由开放艺术空间（Arte Abierto）和索多·马达莱诺建筑事务所（Sordo Madaleno Arquitectos）委托创作，从安塔拉的花园、广场和步行长廊上都可以看到。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《墨西哥城滑梯》装置高度从39英尺到125英尺不等，长度从102英尺到295英尺不等。全部四条螺旋滑梯均向公众开放，允许四人同时从家庭式餐厅、谷歌办公室、瑰丽酒店和开放艺术空间（Arte Abierto Art Space）等不同入口滑下。所有四条滑梯都在同一个出口结束。这位艺术家表示，他希望这一装置能成为参与者和观众的“平衡器”，以及“在原本清醒的头脑中产生的一种丰满的惊慌”。2015年，霍勒在接受《卫报》采访时曾表示，“一个人在滑梯上滑行时不可能不微笑。”", "links": [{"text": "The Guardian", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign/2015/may/17/carsten-holler-travel-down-a-slide-without-smiling-decision"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "霍勒的这件装置是他自1998年开始的一系列持续创作的项目的一部分。这些滑梯的不同变体曾在世界各地亮相，包括伦敦泰特现代美术馆的《试验场》（Test Site，2006）、纽约新美术馆的《维多利亚滑梯》（Victoria Slide，2011）、莱茵河畔魏尔维特拉园区的《维特拉滑梯塔》（Vitra Slide Tower，2014）、佛罗伦萨斯特罗齐宫的《佛罗伦萨实验滑梯》（Florence Experiment Slides，2018）以及哥本哈根丹麦建筑中心的《DAC滑梯》（DAC Slide，2020）。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Belgian artist Carsten Höller ’s giant, spiraling silver slides have made their way to Arte Abierto Polanco in Mexico City as part of a permanent installation.

The large-scale installation, titled Mexico City Slides (2026), features four spiral slides integrated into Antara, an upscale open-air shopping mall that houses retail, dining, entertainment, offices and public space. Höller’s installation was commissioned by Arte Abierto and Sordo Madaleno Arquitectos and can be seen from Antara’s gardens, plazas and pedestrian promenade.

The Mexico City Slides installation ranges from 39 to 125 feet in height and 102 to 295 feet in length. All four spiral slides are open to the public and allow four people to ride simultaneously from various entrances such as the family-style restaurants, the Google offices, the Rosewood Hotel, and the Arte Abierto Art Space. All four slides end at the same exit. The artist said he wanted the installation to be an “equalizer” and a “voluptuous panic upon an otherwise lucid mind” for participants and viewers. In 2015, Höller told The Guardian that it’s “impossible to travel down a slide without smiling.”

Höller’s installation is part of a work-in-progress franchise that he started in 1998. Different variations of the slides have appeared across the world, from Test Site (2006) at Tate Modern in London, Victoria Slide (2011) at the New Museum in New York, Vitra Slide Tower (2014) at the Vitra Campus in Weil am Rhein, Florence Experiment Slides (2018) at Palazzo Strozzi in Florence and DAC Slide (2020) at the Danish Architecture Centre in Copenhagen.

Take the rule-busting, category-smashing, one-of-a-kind-because-you’ve-never-seen-anything-of-its-kind “ You Can See Everything ,” a movie that in one weekend has turned the movie landscape topsy-turvy.

“You Can See Everything” is such an unprecedented cinematic wild card that as you watch it, the very question of what it is makes the movie itself a disruptor. It’s a documentary…made by a prankish cringe comedian…about a notorious white-collar criminal…that plays as a piece of hangout-movie vérité…until the actress who played the white-collar criminal in a TV series actually shows up…at which point the psychodramatic circus is just getting started.

This past weekend, “You Can See Everything” made $15 million on 800 screens (complete with 2,000 sold-out shows). That made it the most successful opening for a non-music documentary since Michael Moore’s “Fahrenheit 9/11,” 22 years ago. Yet even those numbers don’t tell the story of how “You Can See Everything” has injected itself into the cultural bloodstream — and is reconfiguring the movie world. People are rushing to see it almost as a kind of mission. Audiences are alive to it; the film is so full of revelation and new-paradigm entertainment value that people often say it exceeds their expectations. This, in a word, is everything a great movie should be: an experience unlike one you’ve had before, one that lures and enthralls you, and that leaves you feeling different when it’s over.

The film’s box-office numbers are likely to shoot up in its second weekend, when it expands to a full national release. And there’s every chance that the numbers could continue to go up for a week or two after that, the way they did with “Obsession.” The excitement that surrounds “You Can See Everything” rhymes with the out-of-the-box quality that drew people in hordes over the summer to see “Obsession” and “Backrooms.” This was a new kind of audience: a new demo, a new consciousness, a crystalization of the possibility that we might be on the cusp of a new “film generation.” That’s an old term (from the 1970s), one that desribed how the first generation to grow up with movies as their transcendent art form embraced them in a new way, like rock ‘n’ roll — not just as entertainment or even as art but as a fundamental expression of who they were .

Watching “You Can See Everything,” people see themselves reflected in the post-ironic deadpan of Nathan Fielder , who is 42 and represents, from his television shows, a novel mode of fucking with people that’s intricate in its cleverness yet bizarrely honest. Having his close-up conversations with Elizabeth Holmes , he’s wily and detached, but he’s also a straight-shooter, asking rigorous questions about what we want to know: how Holmes could have lied the way she did, and, if she claims (as she does throughout the film) that she wasn’t lying, how she could possibly believe that. The movie, in a sense, is a cosmic meditation on lying. (Holmes sounds as monomaniacal, and as hard to fathom, in her systematic delusions as Donald Trump.) I think the Elizabeth Holmes showcased in “You Can See Everything” is a quintessential example of the human being as corporate performer — she’s doing a dance of put-on earnestness, and her act is so good that Fielder meets his match in attempting to unmask it. The film is an almost dreamlike duel of egos.

By making a movie in which he and his directing partner, Lance Oppenheim, literally didn’t know where they were going, Nathan Fielder has given us a documentary drama that’s all about discovery . That’s what gives “You Can See Everything” its cathartic existential entertainment value. Like “Pulp Fiction,” it seems to be doing nothing less than reinventing what a movie can be. And the outpouring of adoration — and ticket sales — is already so undeniable that I think it’s all but certain that “You Can See Everything” will wind up being the first documentary to be nominated for best picture at the Oscars .

Here’s how that would work. Right now, the film is still forging its path, but I’d wager that it has a solid shot of being named best picture by one or more of the critics’ groups (the New York Film Critics Circle, the Los Angeles Film Critics Association, the National Board of Review, and so on). That would establish its credibility as a work of cinematic art. The Oscar voters aren’t beholden to the critics, but they often follow their lead. It’s been a long time, in fact, since these two pools of tastemakers existed in any true opposition. (I know more than one critic who thinks that it’s the job of year-end critics’ voting to move the needle on the Oscars.) Voting aside, the movie is sure to top many critics’ 10 Best lists, and by the time that happens it will likely have made $100 million at the box office. Its mainstream cultural status as one of the best pictures of the year will, at that point, be undeniable. And if and when it’s nominated for best picture, that will be a ground-shifting moment.

But here’s why I think “You Can See Everything” is also a serious contender to win. This is not an Oscar odds column, and I’m not going to try and parse the chances of “You Can See Everything” next to every film that’s been floated as a contender, from “La Bola Negra” to “Artificial” to “Project Hail Mary” to “I Play Rocky” to the yet-to-be-seen “Dune: Part Three.” But I will use “The Odyssey” as a front-running standard bearer.

In many quarters, “The Odyssey” has acquired an aura of inevitability. It’s the big-vision version of what movies can be, and at a casual glance it connected on every level: with the critics, at the box office, as a must-see cultural phenomenon. At the same time, I think it’s a vulnerable front-runner (in a way that the last Christopher Nolan Oscar movie, “Oppenheimer,” was not), because there are a great many people who are less than in love with it.

If “The Odyssey” wins, it will not be a surprise. It will feel very much like a traditional Oscar victory, the least disruptive one possible. But we are now in an era of disruption — and, quite strikingly, we’re in a year when disruption (from AI or wherever) isn’t just threatening the film industry. It’s looming up as one of the forces that could save it. By the time of Oscar night, “You Can See Everything” may have emerged as the year’s quintessential example of what a movie can be: an ecstatic disruption, an adventure of the spirit, one that wakes you up and startles you, that makes you want to see it again (I’m still working up the courage to go a second round with “The Odyssey”), and one that unites the audience in the feeling of having experienced something uncanny. Something we haven’t seen before. The reason I predict “You Can See Everything” will triumph at the Oscars is that anyone who votes for it won’t just be voting for best picture — they’ll be voting for the future.

article_text:
For more than two decades, Melissa Anderson has been one of New York City’s most important film critics—and one of Film Comment’s favorite writers. From her start as a freelancer in the 2000s, through her staff positions at Time Out , The Village Voice , and most recently 4Columns, she has regaled readers with her peerless wit, her attunement to desire, especially queer desire, and her facility for writing about actors. A new book published by The Film Desk—evocatively titled The Hunger: Film Writing, 2012–2024 —offers an invaluable compilation of Melissa’s writing.

Film Comment editors Clinton Krute and Devika Girish invited Melissa on this week’s episode to talk about her formative experiences of film and film criticism, her development as a writer and editor, and the genesis of this new collection.

Im Drama „ Block 10 “ geht es um den berüchtigten Bau im Konzentrationslager Auschwitz, der für unmenschliche Medizinexperimente diente. Der jüdische Gynäkologe Maximilian Samuel wird dabei gezwungen, die NS-Ärzte zu unterstützen. Für das Projekt recherchierte Produzentin und Drehbuchautorin Alice Brauner jahrelang. Regisseur Marcus O. Rosenmüller entwickelte gemeinsam mit Brauner eine dokumentarische Annäherung und traf sorgsame ästhetische Entscheidungen.

Der filmische Umgang mit der Shoah ist prekär. In dem Moment, in dem man Kunstfilme macht, wird die Realität verfremdet. In dem Moment, in dem man Spielfilme macht, wird sie banalisiert. Wie haben Sie das gelöst?

Marcus O. Rosenmüller : Dieses Thema verbietet eine Ästhetisierung und eine künstlerische Überhöhung! Deswegen habe ich im Drehbuch von Alice Brauner alles gestrichen, was in Richtung künstlerische Ausschmückung oder illustrative Bilder geht. Es gibt deshalb nur die Perspektive auf das Gebäude, wenn die Frauen zum Block 10 geführt werden, und die Perspektive innerhalb des Gebäudes. Ein Kameraflug über das Stammlager Auschwitz beispielsweise hätte nicht der Perspektive der Menschen entsprochen, die das erlebt haben. Ich habe den Film auch nicht in Schwarz-weiß gedreht, weil dadurch eine Distanzierung stattgefunden hätte. Ich will den Zuschauer dazu zwingen, hinzusehen, was im Block 10 wirklich passiert ist.

Über „The Zone of Interest" von Jonathan Glazer

Der Film beginnt mit einem klassischen Bild an der Rampe, erst danach finden Sie eine eigene Bildsprache.

Rosenmüller: Mir war klar, dass die Szene an der Bahnstrecke eher Standard ist. Hätten wir die Szene anders umgesetzt, wäre es wiederum eine Kunstvariante dessen gewesen. Mir war im Anschluss wichtig, dass wir in dem Moment, wo wir mit den Frauen das Gebäude betreten und die Tür hinter ihnen zufällt, in der Block-10-Welt sind und sie dann auch nicht mehr verlassen. Am Anfang erkundet die Kamera von Peter Krause den Raum, danach gibt es keine großen Raumtotalen mehr, damit man sich wieder auf die Menschen und ihre Gefühlswelt konzentrieren kann.

Den Frauen wurden in Block 10 bei der Registrierung die Haare abrasiert, den Schauspielerinnen auch?

Rosenmüller : Es war eine Bedingung, dass wir vielen Schauspielerinnen die Haare abrasieren. Alle sechs griechischen Frauen, deren Ankunft wir zeigen, mussten die Haare verlieren. Es ist ein entmenschlichender Prozess, den wir bei zwei von ihnen direkt im Film sehen. Die Tränen, die in dem Moment fließen, sind echt.

Einige Schauspielerinnen haben das erste Mal eine Rolle gespielt. Wie haben Sie besonders diese Frauen geschützt?

Rosenmüller : Wir hatten bereits während der Castingphase Madli Moos, unsere Intimitätskoordinatorin, dabei. Sie hat mit jeder einzelnen Schauspielerin Gespräche geführt und alle gut aufgefangen. Ich habe noch nie einen Film gemacht, bei dem ich so viel geprobt und Gespräche geführt habe, um alle Schauspielerinnen und Schauspieler auf den Dreh vorzubereiten. Ich habe auch am Set versucht, den Schauspielerinnen ein Gefühl von Vertrauen und Sicherheit zu geben, und ihnen vermittelt, dass das, was wir am Set machen, wirklich authentisch sein muss. In einigen Momenten mussten sich einige von ihnen wirklich überwinden. Das weiß ich sehr zu schätzen.

Die Frauen liegen auf einem OP-Tisch und ihre Bäuche werden – geschützt von Prothesen – aufgeschnitten, um im Film einen Eierstock zu entfernen. Wie haben Sie diese Szenen umgesetzt und wie haben sie auf die Frauen gewirkt?

Rosenmüller: Der OP-Tisch war so gebaut, dass die jeweilige Schauspielerin wie ein S darin lag, und der künstliche Bauch auf ihren Körper aufgelegt wurde, der durch eine Metallplatte unter der Prothese geschützt war. Als Christian Berkel , der Maximilian Samuel spielt, das Skalpell in die Hand genommen hat, um den künstlichen Bauch einer Schauspielerin aufzuschneiden, hat sie eine Panikattacke bekommen und hyperventiliert. Bei der Vorstellung, dass Christian Berkel jetzt in ihren Körper schneidet, wäre sie am liebsten aufgesprungen und rausgerannt. Ich bin dann mit unserer Intimitätskoordinatorin zu ihr hingegangen, wir haben beide ihre Hand genommen und ihr gesagt: „Wir unterbrechen noch mal ein paar Minuten und reden jetzt erst mal ein bisschen.“ Ich wollte ihr in dem Moment nicht das Gefühl geben, dass wir unser Tagespensum schaffen müssen. Sondern, dass sie uns vertrauen kann.

Das zeigt einem auch, dass man – selbst wenn es fiktiv ist – immer noch berührt und verletzt werden kann.

Rosenmüller: Absolut. Ich wollte auf gar keinen Fall eine unwürdige, unmenschliche Atmosphäre am Set haben, damit es „echt“ wirkt. Ich wollte einen respektvollen und menschlichen Umgang herstellen, weil ich auch eine Verantwortung gegenüber den jungen Frauen gespürt habe. Ich wollte nicht, dass sie durch die Dreharbeiten traumatisiert werden. Also habe ich etwa zehn Tage lang die Szenen, in denen es um gynäkologische Eingriffe, um körperliche Gewalt, um OPs geht, mit allen Beteiligten intensiv geprobt. Ich wollte nicht, dass sich eine Frau auf den gynäkologischen Stuhl setzen muss, und dann kommt Axel Prahl kurz vor dem Dreh und sagt: „Ich spiele hier den Arzt. Machen Sie bitte mal die Beine breit.“ Hätte sich eine Frau nicht auf diesen Stuhl setzen wollen, hätte ich es auch respektiert. Wäre das passiert, hätte ich den Drehtag abgebrochen, aber auf so eine Situation wollte ich es nie ankommen lassen. Durch die Proben kannten sich alle und sind vertrauensvoll miteinander umgegangen. Jeder wusste, wer was als nächstes macht.

Bezeichnend ist die riesige Spritze von Prof. Dr. Clauberg, mit der er im Film Kontrast- oder Sterilisationsmittel in die Gebärmutter injiziert. Haben Sie die Realität durch bestimmte Bilder größer gedacht?

Rosenmüller : Ich habe auf illustrative Zwischenschnitte auf medizinische Geräte verzichtet. Alles musste im Kontext der Handlung passieren, um authentisch zu bleiben. Die Spritze kommt in dem Moment ins Bild, in dem die Häftlingsschwester sie aufzieht und dann an Clauberg weiterreicht. Es gibt keine effektvollen Zeitlupenaufnahmen, wie die blutige Spritze in die Schale fällt, sondern nur einen klinischen, fast schon nüchternen Blick auf das Geschehen.

Wir haben beim Drehen die einzelnen Szenen immer aus der Perspektive entweder der Täter oder des Täters, eines Opfers oder eines dieser Funktionshäftlinge – mit anderen Worten der Mitläufer – gezeigt. Den ersten gynäkologischen Eingriff zeigen wir nur aus dem Blickwinkel von Clauberg. Diese perspektivische Erzählweise haben wir während der Dreharbeiten konsequent durchgeführt. Im Schnitt haben wir dann den Fokus auf bestimmte Perspektiven gelegt, zum Beispiel was diese Situation mit einem Menschen macht, der sie beobachtet und eben nicht eingreift.

Wir lernen die Frauen nie richtig kennen, obwohl sie im Fokus stehen …

Rosenmüller: Das liegt natürlich auch an der „fremd“ wirkenden Sprache [ Anm. : Judäo-Spanisch oder Ladino genannt]. Es gibt eigentlich nur eine Szene, in der die Frauen das Gefühl haben, dass sie ganz unter sich sind. Sie liegen dann in ihren Betten, unterhalten sich und eine von ihnen stimmt ein jiddisches Partisanenlied an. Da befreien sie sich für den Moment. Ansonsten herrschte bei allen das gleiche Gefühl – dass ihre Chance umso größer ist, je unauffälliger sie sich verhalten. Der Informationsaustausch war nur knapp und rudimentär, um in Ruhe gelassen zu werden. Jeder Tag, an dem sie nicht herumkommandiert wurden, war für die Frauen ein vergleichsweise guter Tag.

Eine gewisse Wiederholung braucht man, um von Routine zu erzählen. Andererseits schwächen Redundanzen den Eindruck. Wie haben Sie diese Balance gefunden?

Rosenmüller: Wir haben von Anfang an gesagt, dass wir einen Film über den Alltag im Block 10 machen werden. Deshalb gibt es im Tages- und Wochenablauf gar keine Dramaturgie mehr. Jeder Tag ist wie der nächste. Es ist irgendwann egal, ob es Tag, Nacht, Montag, Dienstag, Mittwoch ist. Jeder Tag war dort ein Tag, an dem es ums Überleben ging. Das war das einzige Ziel der Frauen in Block 10. Eine Fensterseite war komplett mit Holz vernagelt, damit die Insassen nicht sehen konnten, was im Innenhof zu Block 11, dem sogenannten „Todesblock“, passiert. Das haben wir im Film übernommen. Die Erschießungen, die im Hof stattgefunden haben – das wissen wir auch aus Zeugenaussagen – haben die Frauen nie gesehen. Wenn du permanent hörst, wie Menschen schreien und Körper fallen, es aber völlig anonym bleibt, ist das akustische Folter.

Die Ärztin Dr. Adélaïde Hautval (Bibiana Beglau) führt eine Strichliste. Nach dem ersten Strich folgt kurz darauf ein zweiter … Wenn man genau hinhört, versteht man, dass sie damit die Erschießungen notiert.

Rosenmüller : Das ist nicht erfunden, sondern wurde von Dr. Hautval später erzählt. Irgendwann hatte sie heimlich einen Zettel für ihre Strichliste in der Tasche. Wir wollten aber nicht nur bei den Handlungen, sondern auch bei den Figuren möglichst dokumentarisch bleiben. Deshalb hat Axel Prahl eine gewisse Ähnlichkeit mit Clauberg, auch er hatte eine geringe Körpergröße und kommt somit Axel Prahl körperlich ganz schön nah – auch wenn Clauberg mit 1,55 Meter noch kleiner war und schwerer Alkoholiker. Auch Christian Berkel ähnelt seiner Figur, damit wir möglichst authentisch sein konnten.

Nur im Abspann singt Gregory Krause „El Male Rachamim“, das traditionelle jüdische Totengebet für die Opfer der Shoah, im Film selbst verzichten Sie auf einen klassischen Score. Trotzdem durchzieht den Film eine Art Grundton. Können Sie den Ton näher definieren?

Rosenmüller : Ich brauchte etwas, das im Raum spürbar, aber nicht greifbar ist. Jeder Raum hat sein eigenes Sound-Design, sogenannte „Sound Drones“ oder auch „Sound Cluster“. Das sind künstlich hergestellte Töne, die oszillieren und einen gewissen Bogen spannen, sich aber nie zu einer Melodie entwickeln. Dadurch haben die Räume im Unterbewusstsein unterschiedliche Temperaturen und erzeugen ein unterschiedliches Gefühl. Einen Raum, in dem die sogenannte Röntgenbombe steht, mit der Dr. Schumann Geschlechtsorgane verbrannte, hat unser Szenenbildner Claus-Rudolf Amler zum Beispiel ganz in Weiß gehalten. Dort ist der Ton am technischsten, so dass man das Gefühl hat, dass der Raum unter elektrischer Spannung steht.

Wie hat „Block 10“ auf Sie gewirkt?

Rosenmüller : Im Nachhinein bin ich dankbar, dass ich diesen Film machen durfte, weil er mir Demut im Umgang mit dem, was im Block 10 passiert ist, gelehrt hat.

article_text:
James Longley ’s “ Mohabat ” won the Opus Bonum section at Ji.hlava Documentary Film Festival on Saturday.

Produced by Mohammad Sharif Hotak, Longley and Oscar-winning filmmaker Alex Gibney , it follows a 12-year-old boy Mohabat, whose father dies in a drone strike. Left without parental care, he’s taken to a city orphanage.

“By patiently observing the boy’s interactions with his two older brothers and the routines and rhythms of life in his village school, the film creates a complex and sympathetic portrait of an individual, a family and a community, stripping away the customary clichés,” argued the jury, calling it “meticulously researched and exquisitely crafted.”

Elvis A-Liang Lu’s “Songs From Within” received a special mention and an award for editing, while Nona Giunashvili’s “Sacred Songs” was named Best Central and Eastern European Documentary. Filip Remunda’s “Love Exposed,” Ishtar Yasin Gutiérrez’s “Life Is There,” Ania Winiarska’s “Good Girls” and Diana Martínez’s “19th Floor” were also awarded.

Brydie O’Connor’s “ Barbara Forever ,” about late artist and activist Barbara Hammer, was the winner of Testimonies.

The jury called it a “compelling cinematic study that breaks several taboos simultaneously: lesbian and female emancipation, aging and terminal illness. This exceptionally empathetic film incorporates experimental footage – shot by the protagonist herself over the span of five decades – in a highly creative manner.”

“Connecting with others through art was really at the core of her practice. It’s also why she loved teaching. I definitely try to take at least a page out of Barbara’s book in that regard,” said O’Connor.

“After one screening, a woman came up to me. She said: ‘I’ve never heard of Barbara Hammer. I’m from Texas and I’m not queer. But I was so moved because my father is at the very end of his life, and he keeps telling our family that he’s at peace. After seeing this movie, I finally understand what he’s saying.’”

In the First Lights section, Philipp Fröhlich picked up the main award for “After the Rehearsal.” Dominika Kováčová triumphed with “Elusiveness of Today” for the film’s “gentle ability to take the viewer from the confines of the physical space in which an elderly woman is bound, to the boundless jam of her mental universe, and for the eloquent play of light and accomplished camera work.”

Finally, Martin Páv picked up Czech Joy’s main award for “Glowing,” while Klára Trsková and Anežka Horová were the winners of Exprmntl.cz with “On the Peaks of All the Beech Mountains.”

Their film was praised for “the political courage in recalling one of the many dark chapters in our contemporary history, the relevance in denouncing ethnic cleansing during complex and painful historical moments, and the sophisticated and stirring filmmaking.”

Vietnamese-American filmmaker Trinh T. Minh-ha was given the Contribution to World Cinema Award.

Currently preparing her upcoming film “The Undying Desert,” her first set in the US, she told Variety about her philosophy.

“You set up the rules for yourself. I’m very glad that I was able to stick with the path I chose and not be intimidated by all these oppressive regulations.”

She added: “Cinema is not just an experience for the eyes. It’s an experience for the whole body. When I was first showing ‘Reassemblage,’ someone told me: ‘I’m hearing this film with my eyes and seeing it with my ears.’ I replied: ‘Perfect,’” she said.

“In East Asia, the senses are not that separate. They overlap. A painter is also a musician and a poet. I think it’s the same with film. It’s better to come with an open mind and see how it speaks to you, rather than focusing on what constitutes a ‘good documentary,’ or what its story or message is.”

article_text:
In March, Paramount revealed James Wan’s onboarding to direct a reimagining of South Korean crime actioner The Gangster, The Cop, The Devil for the studio. The project continues to gain steam as Deadline has confirmed Keanu Reeves has entered talks to star.

Details about Wan’s take on the material and the role to be played by Reeves are under wraps. But the John Wick lead will star opposite Don Lee (aka Ma Dong-seok), who reprises his role from the original as crime boss Jang Dong-su.

Keanu Reeves Sets Thriller ‘Kill Current’ As First Pic Under New Label Two Dragonflies, Teaming With The Arena & Zando

Wan is producing alongside Michael Clear and Jason Blum via Blumhouse Atomic Monster, Lee via Big Punch Global, Sylvester Stallone and D. Matt Geller via Balboa Productions, and Chris S. Lee via B&C Group. Lorenzo di Bonaventura is also now on board to produce.

Eric Pearson wrote the latest script, based on previous drafts by Shay Hatten and Brian Helgeland, who exec produces alongside Billy Acumen.

article_text:
Protest Art

The French Student Protesters Subverting Monuments Like It's May 68

Demonstrators are upending the country’s public landmarks to denounce police violence, under-resourced schools, and a worsening cost-of-living crisis.

When students in France took to the streets in 1968 to protest the country's crumbling education system and Gaullist government, they transformed public statues into participants in their cause. After the May 2 shuttering of Paris Nanterre University, where anti-imperialist students began protests in late March that year, demonstrators took to the Sorbonne, where they hung portraits of Karl Marx, Vladimir Lenin, and Chairman Mao Zedong from the 17th-century facade’s pillars and lodged red revolutionary flags into the statues of scientist Louis Pasteur and writer Victor Hugo . During a May 13 demonstration coinciding with a national general strike, other protesters climbed atop Léopold Morice's "Monument à la République" (1883) , which depicts Marianne, the personification of the French Republic, and staked out the artwork as a gathering ground for fellow protesters.

Today, student demonstrators in France are addressing many of the same issues at the heart of May 68, from underresourced schools to a worsening cost-of-living crisis — and are similarly incorporating public statues, monuments, and culturally significant sites into their actions. Earlier this month, protesters draped the "Monument à la République" in a white garment reading, "Neglected high schools, youth sacrificed," denouncing poor labor conditions, staff shortages, and grueling hours in the education system.

On October 19, dozens of students from the École du Louvre, a higher education arts institution in the Louvre Palace in Paris, blocked the main entrance of the Louvre Museum . And in Marseille, a separate group knocked a bust of Marianne to the floor after breaking into Marseille City Hall.

Elsewhere, protesters have dressed statues in garments referencing other social movements, making broader, historical appeals to France’s long protest tradition. On October 17, organizers gave Marianne a wardrobe change, opting for a yellow vest bearing the message, "2026: The police mutilates high schoolers." A reference to the self-described gilets jaunes (“yellow vests”) who took to the streets in 2018–20 in protest of rising fuel prices and the unaddressed plights of ordinary citizens, the display underscored the longstanding and growing fissures between the public and police, who have overwhelmingly arrested minors and injured hundreds of students since protests began. French rights groups and lawyers have accused police of inflicting " war-like injuries " on teenagers: Riot officers maimed a 14-year-old boy with a tear gas grenade in a Parisian suburb and beat others with batons, among other violent methods.

Demonstrators at the Place de la République streaked the eyes of the allegorical maidens Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity (personifications of the French Revolution slogan and national motto of France) with black tears, suggesting the country’s detachment from the progressive principles and actions fought for in the late 18th-century revolution, when civilians toppled statues of the old monarchic order or replaced them with democratic symbols.

article_text:
The Fine Arts Work Center (FAWC) in Provincetown, Massachusetts, and the Walker Youngbird Foundation will jointly launch a new residency program for Native artists beginning next spring.

Called the Walker Youngbird Native Artist Residency, the initiative will bring a Native artist to FAWC for four weeks (May 23–June 19). The Walker Youngbird Foundation will provide $10,000 for the inaugural year, $2,500 of which will go to the artist as a stipend. The chosen artist will also receive a private apartment and a 400-square-foot studio during their stay, as well as access to FAWC’s broader creative community and a closing public program.

“Provincetown is an epicenter for art in the United States,” Reid Walker, the foundation’s founder, told ARTnews . “We couldn’t think of a better spot than Provincetown to immerse a Native artist in a community that has such a long history, established presence, and great framework.”

FAWC executive director Sharon Polli said that over the past few years she has been “thinking about how we can open up that legacy—open up the opportunity to be in this place that sits at the epicenter of such an important art history—to the widest possible network of artists and writers who could really benefit from being in this landscape.”

They began thinking about “whose voices are missing and who might we most want to reach—and we can’t do that alone.” In the Walker Youngbird Foundation, they found a perfect partner: “There was no one better positioned to help us do that with intention, with care, and with real thought than Reid and his team.”

FAWC was founded in 1968 by a group of artists, including Robert Motherwell, to support artists and writers by giving them time and space to focus on their practice without pressure to produce anything. In 2024, the Motherwell estate gave $200,000 to the organization to support its months-long fellowship program, as well as its shorter summer workshops and residencies.

The latter program, which can last from two weeks to a month, helps “us reach a lot of artists that might not be able to spend seven months here and might need different things at different stages of their career,” Polli said.

No matter the length of the stay, Polli said, the emphasis is on letting artists and writers have “the opportunity to take risks, to experiment, to pilot new things and maybe fail, and to take their work in surprising new directions,” she said. “The secret sauce of our artist residencies is this idea of having time and space that is completely unrestricted. This resident will step right into that and have that same experience.”

The Walker Youngbird Native Artist Residency is the latest in the namesake foundation’s growing profile in supporting Indigenous artists. Earlier this year, it provided funds to launch Native Neon , a residency for a Native artist to produce a work in neon with Lite Brite Neon Studio in Kingston, New York. For that program, the Walker Youngbird Foundation gave $50,000 to cover production costs, travel, and lodging, and a $10,000 artist stipend.

“Our work really focuses on artists at inflection points, points where they are about to make a move into a new direction or jump into a bigger part of their career,” Walker said. “From my discussions with Native American artists who have done residencies, I’ve heard how important that time is—to reflect, to think about new ideas and new possibilities.”

He added, “The community that Fine Arts Work Center offers is important. It’s not just four weeks. It’s going to hopefully be a community that they will take with them long after they leave Provincetown.”

Applications for the four-week residency will open on October 26 and are open to emerging and mid-career Native and Indigenous artists working in any medium. (Artists must be 18 years or older and live in the US or Canada.) Walker will be joined on the selection committee by Mala Iqbal, an artist who chairs FAWC’s visual arts committee, and artist Duane Slick (Meskwaki and Ho-Chunk), a past FAWC fellow and current FAWC trustee. Per a release, the committee will select one artist “based on the strength and vision of the artist’s work and the potential for the residency to meaningfully advance their practice.”

“Native art is not just a sidebar in contemporary art; it’s a major foundational element, and it should be participating in the conversations that happen in art hot spots like Provincetown,” Walker said.

article_text:
From Tuscany to the Cévennes, and onward to the mist-shrouded landscapes of Iceland, she moves through territories that become spaces of memory.

Created as part of the “Prix Résidence pour la Photographie” awarded by the Fondation des Treilles, Sur l’Épaule du Temps has its roots in a family history and in the singular bond her grandmother shared with two lands: the Cévennes, where she was born, and Tuscany, which she chose as her home. The photographs gathered in these two regions form an inner landscape, suspended between presence and absence, past and present.

In Le Murmure des Égarés , Aurélia Frey sets out, among other things, to follow in the footsteps of the “Islandais” — Breton fishermen who left their homeland for long fishing expeditions in Icelandic waters. Through the landscapes, mists, and northern light, she brings forth the memory of these men and their absences, without seeking to reconstruct their history, but rather allowing what remains of it to emerge.

Her black-and-white analogue photography, created notably using Washi film, lends certain images a distinctive texture. The fibres, irregularities, and imperfections of the medium mingle with the light, contributing fully to their ethereal quality, at times almost painterly.

An exhibition in which landscape becomes a space of passage, where places, memories, and presences echo one another, suspended between reality and the imaginary.

article_text:
Cannes animated comedy “ Jim Queen ” has picked up a new batch of international sales after screening at the Busan International Film Festival , its first outing in Asia.

Global Constellation , the sales arm of pan-European studio Vuelta, has closed deals with Prorom for the Czech and Slovak Republics, Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria. HBO has secured first-window pay-TV and SVOD rights in Eastern Europe. Elsewhere, Folkets Bio has taken Sweden, AS Fidalgo has Norway and Films4You has Portugal, while CDI/LAT-E has acquired Argentina, Chile, Uruguay and Paraguay. A South Korean deal is now in negotiation.

The new territories add to earlier sales to I Wonder Pictures (Italy), O’Brother (Benelux), Capelight Pictures (Germany), Praesens (Switzerland), Polyfilm (Austria), Elastica/Filmin (Spain), Lev Cinema (Israel), Madman (Australia and New Zealand), Photon Films (Canada), Pandora Filmes/Belas Artes Grupo (Brazil), Pimienta Films (Mexico) and Creative Century (Taiwan). Creative Century Distribution will open the film in Taiwanese cinemas on Oct. 23.

For the U.S., Global Constellation is weighing several offers, with a release set for 2027. Jordan Firstman and Matteo Lane were recently unveiled as the English-language voices of Jim and Lucien.

Set in Paris, the story centers on Jim, a gym-obsessed influencer and the most desired man on the city’s gay scene. His status collapses overnight when a strange virus called Heterosis begins converting gay men to heterosexuality. Dropped by his followers and shunned by his circle, Jim has only Lucien on his side, a skinny and fiercely loyal admirer. The pair head into the Marais in search of a renegade doctor who may hold a cure.

The film world premiered at Cannes, where festival chief Thierry Frémaux called the screening “one of the most beautiful in the festival’s history in terms of atmosphere.” The Jokers Films opened it in France on June 17, and it entered the box office chart at No. 3 behind “Toy Story 5” and “Backrooms.” It has since passed 385,000 admissions there and taken more than $3 million.

Reviewing the film for Variety , Guy Lodge wrote : “The humor and storytelling can be likened to ‘South Park’ in their senseless, fast-moving escalation toward absurdity, and the broadly cartoonish animation style – clean lines, popping eyes, flat expanses of color in ’80s mall-decor shades of pink, lilac and spearmint – is a running reminder of just how seriously to take the whole enterprise.”

Nguyen and Athané, both Gobelins graduates, co-wrote the screenplay with Simon Balteaux and Brice Chevillard. Between them they have worked on series, games and features including “The Summit of the Gods,” “Ernest & Celestine,” “The Big Bad Fox and Other Tales,” “The Swallows of Kabul,” “The Rabbi’s Cat” and “The Red Turtle.”

David Alric and Arthur Delabays produced for Paris-based adult animation outfit Bobbypills. The studio’s credits include James Gunn’s DC Studios series “Creature Commandos,” “Captain Laserhawk: A Blood Dragon Remix,” a Netflix series made in partnership with Ubisoft Film & Television, and the Netflix titles “Crisis Jung” and “Vermin.” Umedia (“The Count of Monte Cristo,” “The Night of the Zoocalypse”) co-produced, with backing from Eurimages, the CNC’s Avance sur recettes, the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region, the Charente department and the Réunion region.

Global Constellation was formed in 2025 by combining London’s Film Constellation with Munich-based Global Screen.

article_text:
Conceived by artistic directors Cosmin Costinaș and Inti Guerrero , the 2027 Yokahama Triennale will be titled Whalefall: News and Rumours from the Ocean Floor . The exhibition will take place from 23 April to 12 September at the Yokohama Museum of Art.

This edition’s theme builds on two ocean creatures and phenomena: the oarfish, a deep sea creature whose infrequent rise to the surface has long been interpreted in Japan as a foretelling of disasters; and the whale who, when it dies, sinks to the ocean floor and nourishes an entire ecosystem. The Triennale will take these aquatic occurrences as its central metaphor. Following the idea of the news and rumours carried by the oarfish, the exhibition will consider a series of ocean-based episodes in the history of communication, from the rumours circulated by seafaring missionaries to the undersea cables that power the modern internet. Via a specifically-commissioned architectural intervention by Tange Kenzō, the Yokohama Museum of Art will become the body of a whale, inviting viewers to imagine how new worlds emerge from the ocean floor.

article_text:
Exhibition of the week

LS Lowry The strangest and perhaps most truthful painter of modern Britain gets a thorough looking at. MK Gallery, Milton Keynes, 24 October to 28 February

Also showing

Allen Jones Kinky pop art from the diehard naughty boy of 1960s British painting – the Hockney of Soho? Gazelli Art House, London, until 18 December

Multiplied Wonders Woodcuts by Jacopo de’ Barbari, Albrecht Dürer and more reveal the power of the reproduced image in the Renaissance. British Museum, London, until 21 March

Beyond Bayeux Yinka Shonibare, Hurvin Anderson and others design tapestries in collaboration with Edinburgh’s Dovecot Studios, in a somewhat opportunistically titled show. Guildhall Art Gallery, London, until 21 March

Anne Redpath Landscapes on Skye with white houses and bright green fields tenderly depicted in gouache and watercolour. National, Edinburgh, until 6 December

Image of the week

Sheep dung, snails and mouse brains are all beautiful … if you look closely enough. This artwork could be a newly discovered planet or an abstract piece by Stanley Donwood for Radiohead’s A Moon Shaped Pool, but the truth is tinier: it is the tip of a ballpoint pen, a winning entry from the Nikon Small World photography competition .

What we learned

Bowie, bodybuilders and a blubbering Frenchman have changed the way we see masculinity

Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography at Tate Modern will stop you in your tracks

Photos of bustling dancefloors show a changing America through the decades

Frieze art fair is open, and we’ve identified 10 things worth seeing

Bondi beach in Sydney is alive with sculpture

Designer Kate Faulkner is stepping out of William Morris’s shadow in a show that celebrates her influence on Morris & Co Olivier Mourgue, whose Djinn armchairs featured in 2001: A Space Odyssey, has died Great Pottery Throw Down judge Keith Brymer dressed up for a trip down memory lane

Federico Veronesi’s best photograph is a devastating portrait of a grieving elephant

Artist Tony Albert is reappropriating racist artefacts of Aboriginalia for his show Not a Souvenir in Sydney

after newsletter promotion

A new book documents the key players in Cameroon’s vast visual art history

A Paris exhibition explores Ghana before and after it was ripped to shreds by colonialism

Masterpiece of the week

St Jerome and the Lion: Predella Panel by Fra Filippo Lippi and Workshop, 1455-60

Filippo Lippi was the wild man of early 15th-century Florentine art, if the stories told about him in the Renaissance are anything to go by. It was even said his patron Cosimo de’ Medici had to lock him in the Medici palace to stop his debauchery. There is a core of fact behind the tales, as Filippo – a friar – is known from legal records to have had children with an escaped nun, Lucrezia Buti. Their son Filippino also became an artist. But whatever his life was like, there’s no lack of piety in this painting of the early Christian Jerome, a real historical figure who translated the Bible into Latin. The lion tamely lets the holy man pull a thorn from its paw, in an intricately painted mountainous landscape with a pink church. Jerome concentrates on his work, as you would if you were de-thorning a dangerous big cat. This is just a small panel from the base of an altarpiece but it packs in the emotion and humanity that makes Lippi a great artist, in spite of, or because of, his sins.

article_text:
In Stephanie Ahn’s Bedford Park , Moon Choi plays Audrey, a self-destructive health care worker trapped in a paralyzing relationship with her immigrant parents. The drama, which won the Special Jury Award for Debut Feature at Sundance earlier this year, screened at this year’s Busan International Film Festival ahead of a release from Sony Pictures Classics.

Choi and director Stephanie Ahn appeared at Q&As at the BIFF screenings. Choi was also a member of the Competition Jury, led by Zhang Yimou. She arrived in Busan after a two-week run of The Cherry Orchard at New York’s Park Avenue Armory.

The Film Stage: Bedford Park opens with an intense S&M scene and proceeds through several disturbing moments. How dark were you willing to go?

Moon Choi : To be honest, these are some of my most challenging scenes as an actor. Looking back at my career, I did have some dark or heavily emotional scenes in the past, but what Audrey’s going through in this movie is pretty dark, especially in the beginning. But I don’t really think about it in those terms. I just thought that this is something she is placed into abruptly. Something that she has to go through moment to moment. I didn’t necessarily think: How should I approach this? Should I approach it in a different way from the lighter scenes? I just tried to focus on what she’s actually going through physically and mentally step by step. It was challenging, but I wasn’t uncomfortable about it.

You needed these scenes to define Audrey’s character.

Not only does she go through a miscarriage, but she falls into this habit of self-harming. Meeting up with a stranger, having a one-night stand, having S&M sex, hurting herself with a razor. That’s all very cruel things to do. But when you think about it, there’s something inside her that tries to punish her without being aware of it. Because she thinks that she’s not perfectly being herself. Because she’s trying to make up to her parents’ expectations of who they want her to be. She’s been living her life in a shell of a person for 35 years.

Self-harming, meeting these strangers for violent sex is kind of a way for her to escape. I don’t think she’s enjoying it. She’s hurting herself, punishing herself for not being able to have ownership in her own life.

She’s facing impossible expectations from her parents. No one could live that way. The movie shows how her brother self-medicates in his own way.

Logically, it was hard to follow how she ended up that way, but I talked to Stephanie for years and years about this. After I learned that this is where she’s coming from, then afterwards, it was easier. I wasn’t afraid to be on set in that scene. It was more of the process before going on set that was a little tough for me, to try to really feel grounded as an actor who knows that character thoroughly.

How did this production compare to your films in Korea? Did you consider it a small film?

I’ve done both commercial and indie films in Korea. One really micro-budget film called Our Body cost less than $50,000. But I’ve also done Okja . Deliver Us from Evil was a huge blockbuster action thriller in Korea. This was a rather small production, but it felt pretty good. There was so much trust between Stephanie, the producers, and my co-actors. It was a friendly set, like a family. We did feel rushed at times.

The scenes with my parents, those were shot in two days. We shot from me arriving with a suitcase at the parents, then Audrey getting the note from Eli (played by Son Suk-ku). We couldn’t shoot in order because of the lighting. We’d go from scene 80 or something to scene 3. I had that experience before with micro-budget films.

You can’t really think of the actor’s process in that situation. What’s important is to save time on lighting and setting up. I felt lucky that I was used to that, because let’s say if I’d only done a big TV series or big commercial films back in Korea, I think going through those scenes in such a rush would’ve been very stressful.

A small production can be an advantage because you don’t get distracted by crew members and equipment.

Also, Son Suk-ku and I didn’t really take time to monitor our acting. I know there are actors who want to play back and see every take, we aren’t like that. We trust that when we feel truthful, the camera must have captured it. So, we didn’t necessarily go through playbacks. That saved time. When an actor goes, “Can we stop for a moment and check what we have?”—that’s when you lose time. We were like, if Stephanie says it’s okay, it’s good, and we just move on.

Did you ever run out of time?

No, I don’t think so. Sometimes Stephanie would say okay after two or three takes because it was great. Sometimes she would explore, do five or six takes to see what happens

There’s a scene with Audrey and Eli in the car where we listen to the Rocky theme. It’s a long take. We’re starting to listen to the music, getting immersed in it, feeling something very different with each other than what we felt before. Also being present in the moment, in that close space together. We knew that scene was a little different from other scenes where we cut back and forth. We took some time with that scene. I think it’s the seventh take in the movie.

We shot it in a studio, with the camera starting outside the windshield and then kind of zooming and tracking in together. No cuts. I think it’s a three-minute take. We had the sound people play the song in the car so we could hear it. So, yeah, those scenes take time, but I don’t think we ever went over something like ten takes.

Is there an advantage to working quickly? You have to get everything out there at once.

The thing is, we had so much time for pre-production because I was cast for this part seven years ago. I was working on Korean films and TV series. Whenever I finished a project, I would take time to talk to Stephanie and tell her how my experience went and what I learned from it. Sometimes I would go back to our script and say, “You know, I never thought about this scene in that way, but after finishing this project, now I have more of a sense of it.” You kind of take bits from one project to another, and you learn from this character to that character to build more layers and complexities for Audrey. This was when I was expecting to perform two or three years later when we had the financing ready. We were very frustrated that we didn’t have all of the money, but then I was kind of just thinking, “This will be good for me because I’ll never again have seven years for pre-production for a character.” I literally grew old with her.

When I was cast for the part, I was 30 or 31. Audrey’s supposed to be 36. Stephanie used to say that I looked too young, psychologically and physically. I thought, what difference does it make to be 30 instead of 35? But after 35, you have more life experience in my career, and in my personal life. I found out that Stephanie and I went to the same high school in New Jersey. I lived in the States for three years, from the age of 14 to 17. And that was in Tenafly, a small town in Bergen County, New Jersey.

It’s a beautiful town. But at the time, I thought it was way too much nature. There were deer and rabbits and geese flying around. I came from Seoul, very metropolitan, very crowded. I didn’t speak English. I spent those years learning the language, meeting my first boyfriend, making friends with classmates. Those years really formed me. When I learned that Stephanie went to the same high school, it’s probably why I felt so drawn to the character of Audrey.

Shooting on actual locations helped ground your film. Like that awful shopping mall where Eli works.

The one in Paramus. I used to go there with my mom. My aunt still lives in Paramus. So the shoot was like homecoming for me. The whole experience of being cast in this film, waiting for it to happen, learning about Stephanie’s life and her parents growing old with her, shooting in New Jersey. The whole experience for me as an actor was like a dream come true.

You have a producing credit on the film. You also did still photography.

Originally, Audrey would be drawing with a pad. When Stephanie realized I have a passion for film photography, she was like, “Can you do that actually?” We made that Audrey’s hobby, something she feels very attached to, something that makes her feel like herself. Stephanie wrote this amazing monologue about how Audrey’s father made the family pose in front of his camera, and that’s why she never asks anyone to pose for her.

Bedford Park

Can you talk about being on the Competition jury? This is the first year Busan is an Oscar-qualifying festival.

I felt a lot of pressure when I was asked to be a member of the jury. When I saw the names of the other jurors, I realized I was going to be the only Korean actor. I’ve been in the industry for 17 years, working on everything from indies to blockbusters, in Korea, Japan, and America, so maybe there’s something I can contribute to the team. Also, I can learn from Zhang Yimou or Bi Gan or July Jung, an amazing Korean female director. We had our first meeting yesterday. It was a lot of fun, and we were pretty much aligned. We’re in pretty good shape.

You just finished a run of The Cherry Orchard in New York, playing with Jeon Do-yeon and Park Hae-soo.

We’ve been touring for three years. We started in Seoul, went to Busan, Singapore, Hong Kong, Australia, and finally New York. Usually we’d perform three or four shows at each venue, but in New York we had a two-week run. Sandra Hüller came one night, which thrilled everyone in the cast.

Jeon Do-yeon is also in Possible Love , where she gives a heartbreaking performance.

She’s Korea’s Meryl Streep and Julianne Moore and Nicole Kidman, all combined together. I grew up watching her films. Whenever I told her that, she’s like, “Stop, that makes me feel old.” Working with her was such a big privilege. To be honest, I was so nervous in rehearsals I couldn’t look her in the eye. When she’s acting, she’s so vulnerable, and she opens all channels to you without any prejudice and without any calculation. She makes your acting better because she’s so good.

She’s willing to be the character and not protect herself as an actress, not try to hold onto something that would let viewers know she’s not really that person.

That’s the kind of actor I aspire to be. She gives everything to the audience. She’s vulnerable, and therefore lovable, but also she’s so human. In Possible Love , she wants to set herself free and set her husband free, and she does everything she can to get there. But she can’t help watching these rich people being nice but also condescending. They’re not your friends. They say they love you, but do they? Is that even possible? The layers that Lee Chang-dong built in that film were so amazing to watch that after the credits were over, I couldn’t get up from my seat.

Bedford Park screened at the 2026 Busan International Film Festival and opens March 5, following a qualifying run beginning Dec. 11 at NYC’s Village East and LA’s Laemmle NoHo 7.

EXCLUSIVE: Cory Michael Smith is the latest to join the ensemble cast of Ari Aster ‘s next thriller Scapegoat , starring Scarlett Johansson . The film also stars Jacob Elordi, Jude Law, Ella Purnell, Caleb Landry Jones and Samba Schutte. Aster is directing from a script he wrote. A24, who has released Aster’s past four films, is the distributor.

Aster and partner Lars Knudsen will produce through their Square Peg banner.

While the plot is being kept under wraps, some have speculated it’s about a doctor who operates on an internet-famous person. Others say it’s sci-fi romance, and some have said it’s more of a traditional drama for Aster. As of now, there is no consensus on the movie’s details, according to insiders.

Deadline first reported earlier this year that this would be Aster’s next film after the director had taken his time deciding on what would be his follow-up to Eddington .

Watch on Deadline

Smith is coming off his acclaimed performance in the HBO movie Mountatinhead , which also starred Steve Carell and Ramy Youssef. He can currently be seen opposite Dakota Fanning and Jake Johnson in The Sun Never Sets.

Next up, he has the A24 pic Slayground from director Jeremy Saulnier. That film bows January 29. He Is repped by UTA and Circel M&P.
